The Opportunity Cost of De-Extinction

Report by Marcus Ellery and Hana Okafor · March 3, 2026

Share: X LinkedIn Email

Summary

Public and private funders have committed large sums to reviving extinct species. This report asks what that money would have bought if it had gone to protecting species that are still alive, and finds that the comparison is rarely made before a revival program is funded.

Key findings

  • Revival programs and habitat protection draw on overlapping donor pools in four of the six regions studied.
  • Funding announcements for revival programs almost never state what the money would otherwise have protected.
  • Agencies that lost private funding to revival programs cut field staff before they cut research.

Why the comparison matters

A revived species needs somewhere to live. If the habitat that once supported it has been lost, the revived animal becomes a permanent ward of the program that created it, and its long-term cost belongs on the same ledger as its creation.

The question is not whether we can bring a species back, but what we stop doing in order to try.

We recommend that every public grant for a revival program be accompanied by an estimate of the habitat protection the same sum would fund, published with the award.

About the authors

Marcus Ellery is a senior fellow at the Harwell Institute. Hana Okafor directs its biodiversity program.
